overview: This single-page file register inventories 1936 State Department papers concerning the strict Japanese enforcement of navigation and fortified-area regulations in colonial Taiwan (Formosa), the Penghu (Pescadores) Islands, and other Japanese territorial waters. The listed correspondence arose from the seizure of the Danish steamship NICOLINE MAERSK and an earlier case involving the JUNO, as well as complaints by Edwin H. Duff and the Oceanic and Oriental Navigation Company that ships seeking emergency refuge risked confiscation. The register traces consideration of an American diplomatic protest, inquiries into British action, correspondence between the British ambassador and the Japanese Foreign Office, and the Far Eastern Division’s conclusion that the United States lacked a basis for protest.

subfiles.title: List of papers on navigation laws and regulations in Taiwan and Formosa
subfiles.about: A register summarizes the correspondence filed concerning Japanese restrictions on foreign vessels entering closed or fortified waters around Taiwan, the Penghu Islands, and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The register records papers dated from February through September 1936, beginning with a warning against entering or anchoring near the Penghu Islands and references to the NICOLINE MAERSK and JUNO cases. It then traces Edwin H. Duff’s complaint that the enforcement regime could expose vessels seeking emergency refuge to confiscation, the Department’s inquiry into British action, and reports from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew about a British diplomatic approach. The final listed memorandum, prepared in the Far Eastern Division by Turner, concludes that the United States had no basis for a formal diplomatic protest.

interest: Although it contains no substantive correspondence itself, this register provides a compact chronology and roadmap to a broader diplomatic case concerning the collision between maritime emergencies and Japanese military-security restrictions. It is especially useful for linking the NICOLINE MAERSK and JUNO incidents to lobbying by a shipping company, British representations in Tokyo, and the State Department’s decision not to protest. Its cross-references and document numbers may help historians locate related papers elsewhere in the decimal file.
